regions.name: Frontal lobe
regions.supply: Anterior cerebral artery (medial surface) and middle cerebral artery (lateral surface)
regions.functions: Planning, judgment, attention and drive; voluntary movement (premotor cortex); expressive speech in the dominant inferior frontal gyrus (Broca area); frontal eye fields turn the eyes to the opposite side.
regions.normal: Low-voltage fast (beta) activity, especially anteriorly. Eye-blink and eye-movement potentials appear in the frontopolar channels.
regions.lesion: Abulia and personality change, contralateral weakness or slowed movement, expressive aphasia in the dominant hemisphere, gaze deviation. Focal polymorphic delta over the frontal region, and attenuated fast activity over a destructive lesion.
regions.seizure: Often brief, frequent, stereotyped and out of sleep; hypermotor or tonic posturing, vocalization, little postictal confusion. Complex bizarre movements are easily mistaken for non-epileptic events.
regions.eegNote: F7 and F8 overlie both the inferior frontal gyrus and the anterior temporal lobe, and are listed with the temporal region on this page. Interictal spikes are often scarce or absent because much of the frontal cortex is deep, medial or inferior. Ictal EEG is often hidden by movement and muscle artifact. Bilateral synchronous discharges can occur through rapid spread across the corpus callosum.

regions.name: Central (sensorimotor) cortex
regions.supply: Middle cerebral artery for the face and arm; anterior cerebral artery for the leg on the medial surface
regions.functions: Precentral gyrus is motor and postcentral gyrus is sensory, arranged as a map of the opposite body (the homunculus): the leg is medial near Cz, the hand lies under C3 and C4, and the face is lateral and low, toward T3 and T4.
regions.normal: Arch-shaped mu rhythm (about 8 to 10 Hz) over the central region, which persists with eye opening and is blocked by movement or the thought of movement of the opposite side.
regions.lesion: Contralateral weakness and sensory loss. The mu rhythm is lost over a destructive lesion. Focal delta can occur over it.
regions.seizure: Focal motor seizures with clonic jerking that can march along the body (Jacksonian march), or sensory symptoms such as tingling. Rolandic epilepsy of childhood arises here.
regions.eegNote: Centrotemporal spikes with a horizontal dipole (negative centrally, positive frontally) are the typical childhood focus. A skull defect gives a breach rhythm: a sharp, mu-like, higher-amplitude fast rhythm over the defect.

regions.name: Temporal lobe
regions.supply: Middle cerebral artery (lateral temporal) and posterior cerebral artery (mesial and inferior temporal)
regions.functions: Hearing and auditory association (superior temporal gyrus), comprehension of speech in the dominant hemisphere (Wernicke area), memory and emotion (hippocampus and amygdala in the mesial temporal lobe).
regions.normal: Mixed low-voltage theta and alpha. Wicket spikes and small sharp spikes of drowsiness are normal variants, and are often mistaken for temporal epileptiform discharges.
regions.lesion: Receptive aphasia on the dominant side, memory loss, auditory and superior visual-field defects (a quadrant loss). Focal polymorphic delta over the lesion and, in epilepsy, intermittent temporal rhythmic delta.
regions.seizure: Rising epigastric sensation, fear, deja vu, smell or taste aura, then staring, lip-smacking and hand automatisms with later confusion. Lateral temporal seizures can start with auditory or language symptoms.
regions.eegNote: Anterior temporal sharp waves with the maximum at F7/F8 or the anterior temporal electrodes, best seen in drowsiness and sleep. Ictal onset is often rhythmic theta (5 to 7 Hz) that grows in amplitude and slows as it spreads.

regions.name: Parietal lobe
regions.supply: Middle cerebral artery (lateral) and anterior cerebral artery (medial); watershed with the posterior cerebral artery behind
regions.functions: Somatic sensation and spatial awareness. Neglect of the opposite side follows a non-dominant lesion; the dominant angular and supramarginal region supports calculation, writing, finger recognition and left-right orientation (Gerstmann syndrome).
regions.normal: Posterior alpha spreads forward into the parietal channels and blocks with eye opening.
regions.lesion: Sensory loss, neglect, apraxia, and a lower-quadrant field defect from the upper optic radiation. Focal delta and loss of normal alpha over the lesion.
regions.seizure: Sensory or somatosensory auras, a sense of body distortion or vertigo; spread to the temporal or frontal lobes often gives the visible seizure.
regions.eegNote: Posterior-quadrant discharges are often hard to localize because the lesion lies between the central, temporal and occipital fields. Compare the amplitude of homologous parietal channels.

regions.name: Occipital lobe
regions.functions: Primary visual cortex around the calcarine fissure. Each side serves the opposite visual field.
regions.normal: Posterior dominant rhythm (alpha) on eye closure; it blocks with eye opening. Posterior slow waves of youth and lambda waves are normal.
regions.lesion: A contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with the macula spared because it has dual blood supply. The alpha rhythm may be reduced over the lesion. In the Bancaud phenomenon the alpha on the lesion side fails to block when the eyes open, while the normal side blocks, so the two sides become asymmetric. Focal occipital delta may appear.
regions.seizure: Elementary visual hallucinations (coloured flashes, circles), blindness or eye deviation. Autonomic features such as vomiting occur in early-onset childhood occipital epilepsy.
regions.eegNote: Occipital spikes in childhood, which may vanish when the eyes are open (fixation-off sensitivity) and appear in eye closure or darkness.

territories.name: Anterior cerebral artery
territories.area: Medial frontal and parietal lobes, including the leg area of the motor and sensory cortex
territories.deficit: Contralateral leg weakness greater than arm, abulia, urinary incontinence
territories.eeg: Parasagittal (Fz, Cz, F3, F4, C3, C4) delta and attenuation; midline findings can look bilateral

territories.name: Middle cerebral artery
territories.area: Most of the lateral hemisphere: face and arm motor and sensory areas, Broca and Wernicke areas in the dominant hemisphere, the parietal association cortex
territories.deficit: Contralateral face and arm weakness and sensory loss, aphasia (dominant) or neglect (non-dominant), gaze preference toward the lesion
territories.eeg: Focal polymorphic delta over the central and temporal region, loss of mu and spindles on that side, reduced amplitude of faster activity. These findings are largest in the first days and often fade as the infarct matures.

territories.name: Posterior cerebral artery
territories.area: Occipital lobe, inferior and mesial temporal lobe, and the thalamus
territories.deficit: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia (macula often spared), memory loss from mesial temporal involvement, thalamic sensory loss
territories.eeg: Occipital delta and alpha attenuation on the side of the lesion; temporal slowing if mesial temporal lobe is involved

territories.name: Vertebrobasilar (brainstem and thalamus)
territories.area: Brainstem reticular activating system, thalamus, cerebellum
territories.deficit: Impaired arousal or coma, cranial nerve and eye-movement signs, crossed deficits. A pontine lesion can cause a locked-in state with preserved awareness.
territories.eeg: Frontally predominant alpha or theta activity unreactive to stimuli (alpha coma, alpha-theta coma) in a comatose patient, or a usually normal or near-normal, reactive EEG in a locked-in patient

territories.name: Border zones (watershed)
territories.area: Cortex between territories, for example between the ACA and MCA, and between the MCA and PCA behind
territories.deficit: Infarcts after low blood pressure; shoulder-and-thigh weakness, visual and parietal syndromes
territories.eeg: Slowing and amplitude asymmetry over the parasagittal and posterior parietal regions

generators.title: Where the EEG comes from
generators.text: The scalp EEG records summed postsynaptic potentials (mainly excitatory and inhibitory synaptic currents), not action potentials. Pyramidal neurons in cortical layers III and V line up side by side, so their apical dendrites sum into a dipole. Tens of millions of neurons must be active together, spread across at least several square centimetres of cortex, for the field to reach the scalp.

generators.title: Radial and tangential dipoles
generators.text: Cortex on the crown of a gyrus produces a radial dipole that the scalp electrode sees most clearly. Cortex in the wall of a sulcus produces a tangential dipole, which gives a horizontal field with a negative pole at one electrode and a positive pole at another, as with the rolandic spike: negative centrally and positive frontally.

generators.title: Why the thalamus matters
generators.text: The thalamus acts as a pacemaker and relay. Thalamocortical neurons and the thalamic reticular nucleus form loops with the cortex. Their rhythmic bursts underlie sleep spindles (12 to 14 Hz) and help to produce the alpha rhythm.

generators.title: Slow waves and deafferentation
generators.text: Focal polymorphic delta is produced when the overlying cortex is deafferented by a white-matter or deep lesion; normal sleep delta comes from thalamocortical and cortical networks in a hyperpolarized state. A diffuse white-matter, thalamic or arousal-system disturbance gives generalized slowing.

generators.title: The epileptiform discharge
generators.text: A sudden synchronous depolarization of many neurons (the paroxysmal depolarizing shift) produces the spike. The long hyperpolarization that follows, from inhibition and potassium efflux, produces the after-going slow wave. This is why spikes are often followed by a slow wave.

generators.title: Seizure initiation and spread
generators.text: Seizures arise when excitation (glutamate acting at NMDA and AMPA receptors) outweighs inhibition (GABA) and neurons begin to fire in synchrony. Impaired inhibition, increased excitation, or abnormal ion channel function can all do this. A focus spreads along cortical connections and through the corpus callosum or the thalamus.

generators.title: Generalized spike-and-wave and the thalamocortical loop
generators.text: Absence seizures arise when the thalamocortical loop oscillates abnormally. Low-threshold T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons, together with GABA-B-mediated inhibition of thalamocortical relay neurons by the reticular nucleus, drive a regular 3 Hz cycle, which appears on the scalp as generalized spike-and-wave with abrupt onset and offset.

generators.title: Why age matters
generators.text: The immature brain has more excitatory synapses and less mature inhibition, so it is prone to epileptic spasms and to epileptic encephalopathies. Many childhood syndromes appear at a characteristic age and resolve as the brain matures.

syndromes.name: Early infantile developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (Ohtahara-type)
syndromes.seizure: Tonic spasms, often in clusters, difficult to treat
syndromes.pathophys: Usually a structural brain malformation or a genetic cause. The immature brain cannot sustain a continuous background, so bursts of activity alternate with suppression.
syndromes.eeg: Burst suppression in both waking and sleep. Bursts are high amplitude and mixed with spikes; suppression between them is nearly flat. The pattern can persist unchanged and often evolves into hypsarrhythmia in later infancy.
syndromes.technologist: Record both states and any spasms with time markers. Describe burst and suppression durations; note the medications.
syndromes.label: Ohtahara
syndromes.eegShort: Burst suppression in waking and sleep.

activation.sleep: Record both waking and sleep. Burst suppression that persists in both states is the key finding and separates it from normal trace alternant, which appears only in quiet sleep of the term neonate.
activation.awake: Burst suppression is present awake too, so a short awake segment is informative.
activation.photic: Not useful in a neonate; do not delay the recording for it.

recording.duration: Long enough to include a wake segment, a sleep segment and, ideally, several tonic spasms.
recording.montage: Neonatal or infant montage with wide inter-electrode distances. Use a referential view to show the generalized suppression, and add EMG and respiration channels where available to time spasms.

manifestations: Frequent brief tonic spasms, single or in clusters, often present from the first days or weeks
Spasms occur in both waking and sleep
Severe developmental impairment and hypotonia
Feeding difficulty is common
triggers: Usually spontaneous; spasms occur in both wake and sleep
clinical.exam: Often abnormal, with hypotonia and poor responsiveness.
clinical.imaging: A structural cause such as a cortical malformation is common; genetic causes are also recognized.
clinical.development: Severe impairment from onset or soon after.

course.onset: Neonatal period or first weeks to 3 months of life.
course.progression: The burst-suppression pattern often changes to hypsarrhythmia in later infancy, and some children go on to Lennox-Gastaut syndrome.
course.outcome: Poor; drug-resistant seizures and severe disability are usual, and early mortality is increased.

differential: Early myoclonic encephalopathy - erratic myoclonus rather than tonic spasms; burst suppression is often more marked in sleep and a metabolic cause is common
Normal trace alternant - only in quiet sleep, with normal waking activity and a healthy infant
Hypoxic-ischemic or other acute encephalopathy - burst suppression with a clear acute history, and it may improve
West syndrome - later onset with hypsarrhythmia rather than burst suppression
pearls: Burst suppression in both wake and sleep is abnormal; trace alternant is sleep-only and symmetrical.
The suppression phase is nearly flat; check electrode impedances so that a real flat interval is not confused with a disconnected electrode.
Tonic spasms may coincide with a burst or with a brief attenuation; mark each event with the time.
The pattern may evolve into hypsarrhythmia, so note the infant's age on the tracing.
Record the medication list: some drugs and sedation produce burst suppression too.
syndromes.sceneNote: Burst-suppression tracing: high-amplitude bursts alternating with nearly flat intervals.

syndromes.label: EME
syndromes.name: Early myoclonic encephalopathy (EME)
syndromes.ageText: Neonatal period, usually the first weeks of life (before 3 months)
syndromes.seizure: Erratic, fragmentary myoclonus (often shifting from one body part to another), plus focal motor seizures and later tonic spasms
syndromes.pathophys: Often an inborn error of metabolism (nonketotic hyperglycinemia is a classic example) or a genetic cause, with severe diffuse cortical dysfunction. A structural cause is less common.
syndromes.eeg: Burst suppression with high-amplitude bursts, mixed spikes and sharp waves, and near-flat suppression between them. The pattern is often more obvious in sleep and may be less regular or less continuous awake early on. Erratic myoclonus often has no consistent EEG correlate. The pattern may change to hypsarrhythmia or a multifocal pattern.
syndromes.eegShort: Burst suppression, often more marked in sleep, with erratic myoclonus.
syndromes.technologist: Record both waking and sleep. Time-mark every jerk, add EMG leads if available, and describe burst and suppression durations. Note the medication list.

activation.sleep: The most useful state: burst suppression is often clearest in sleep, so record sleep and compare it with waking.
activation.awake: Record a waking segment too; the pattern may be less continuous when awake.

recording.duration: Long enough to include waking, sleep and a number of myoclonic events.
recording.montage: Neonatal or infant montage with wide inter-electrode distances and a referential view. Add EMG and respiration channels, and use video to match jerks with the EEG.

manifestations: Erratic, fragmentary myoclonic jerks that move between body parts
Focal motor seizures, later tonic spasms
Hypotonia, poor feeding and severe developmental impairment
Onset in the first days to weeks of life
clinical.exam: Severely abnormal, with hypotonia and little interaction.
clinical.imaging: Often normal early on when the cause is metabolic; structural change can be present.
clinical.development: Severe impairment from early life.

course.onset: The neonatal period, often the first weeks of life.
course.progression: The burst-suppression pattern may change to hypsarrhythmia or a multifocal pattern.
course.outcome: Poor; seizures are drug-resistant, disability is severe and early mortality is increased.

differential: Ohtahara syndrome - tonic spasms are dominant, and burst suppression is present awake and asleep
Normal trace alternant - sleep-only and normal when awake, and the infant is well
Metabolic or hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy - can produce a similar tracing, so the history matters
West syndrome - later onset with hypsarrhythmia
pearls: Erratic, migrating myoclonus is the typical seizure type, in contrast to the tonic spasms of Ohtahara syndrome.
Burst suppression is often more obvious in sleep; record both states and compare.
Many myoclonic jerks have no EEG correlate; use EMG and video and mark them anyway.
A metabolic cause is common, so describe the tracing and age exactly and let the physician interpret it.
Both burst-suppression syndromes can change into hypsarrhythmia, which is why the age is noted.
syndromes.sceneNote: Neonatal burst suppression: bursts of about 1.2 s and 1.4 s separated by flat intervals.

syndromes.name: West syndrome (infantile epileptic spasms syndrome)
syndromes.ageText: 1 month to 2 years (most 3 to 12 months, peak 4 to 7)
syndromes.seizure: Epileptic spasms: brief flexor, extensor or mixed jerks in clusters on waking or falling asleep
syndromes.pathophys: Many causes, including structural, genetic, metabolic and hypoxic injury. One hypothesis is an immature brain with abnormal brainstem-cortical interaction.
syndromes.eeg: Hypsarrhythmia: chaotic, high-amplitude (often above 200 uV), asynchronous slow waves with multifocal spikes and no organized background. A spasm is accompanied by a generalized slow wave followed by sudden attenuation of the background (an electrodecrement), often with muscle artifact. In non-REM sleep the pattern is often more evident and may become more bursty (periodic), and it may attenuate in REM sleep.
syndromes.technologist: Mark every spasm with the time, record sleep, and describe the background. Muscle artifact can mimic or hide the electrodecrement.
syndromes.label: West
syndromes.eegShort: Hypsarrhythmia, with an electrodecrement at each spasm.

activation.sleep: The most useful state: hypsarrhythmia is often more evident, and may become bursty, in non-REM sleep. Sleep recording is essential and, ideally, includes an awakening.
activation.awake: The pattern is usually present awake but may be less prominent. Spasms often cluster on waking.
activation.photic: Not a useful activation procedure in this age group.

recording.duration: Long enough to include sleep and ideally a transition on waking, when spasms cluster.
recording.montage: Infant montage with a referential view to show the multifocal, asymmetric spikes. Add deltoid or neck EMG and video to time each spasm.

manifestations: Clusters of brief flexor, extensor or mixed spasms, often on waking
Loss of previously acquired skills, or developmental stall
Reduced eye contact and social smiling
Spasms can be subtle, such as head nods or eye movements
clinical.exam: Depends on the cause; signs of a structural or genetic disorder may be present, and some children appear normal at first.
clinical.imaging: A cause is often found, such as a cortical malformation, hypoxic-ischemic injury, a tuberous sclerosis lesion or a genetic disorder.
clinical.development: Stall or regression is typical.

course.onset: Usually the first year, most often between 3 and 12 months.
course.progression: May evolve into other seizure types, including focal seizures or Lennox-Gastaut syndrome.
course.outcome: Depends mainly on the underlying cause; a symptomatic cause carries a worse outlook. Prompt reporting of the findings matters.

differential: Benign myoclonus of infancy - jerks occur with a normal EEG
Ohtahara syndrome or EME - burst suppression instead of hypsarrhythmia, and onset in the neonatal period
Infantile colic, startle and normal sleep jerks - no EEG change
Dravet syndrome and other infantile epilepsies - different seizure types and EEG
pearls: The classic triad is epileptic spasms, hypsarrhythmia and developmental stall or regression.
Each spasm is accompanied by a generalized slow wave with an electrodecrement; mark it on the tracing.
Sleep should be recorded because hypsarrhythmia can be absent awake or seen only in sleep.
Muscle artifact from a spasm can hide the electrodecrement; use EMG and video.
Hypsarrhythmia may appear modified, asymmetric or only in part; describe what you see.
syndromes.sceneNote: Hypsarrhythmia tracing, with a second view showing a spasm with an electrodecrement.

syndromes.name: Dravet syndrome
syndromes.ageText: Onset in the first year (often about 6 months)
syndromes.seizure: Prolonged febrile or afebrile hemiclonic or generalized clonic seizures, later myoclonic, absence and focal seizures
syndromes.pathophys: Usually a loss-of-function mutation in the SCN1A sodium channel gene, reducing sodium current in inhibitory neurons.
syndromes.eeg: The first EEG may be normal. Later: generalized spike-and-wave and polyspike-wave, focal or multifocal discharges and photosensitivity, with progressive slowing of the background.
syndromes.technologist: Record in sleep; do photic stimulation per protocol with attention to safety, and note any fever or clinical event.
syndromes.label: Dravet
syndromes.eegShort: Generalized and multifocal spike-wave with photosensitivity; the first EEG may be normal.

activation.photic: Photosensitivity and pattern sensitivity occur in a subset, so do photic stimulation per protocol, with attention to safety, and stop at any seizure.
activation.sleep: Sleep may bring out generalized or multifocal discharges and is worth recording.
activation.awake: The first EEG may be normal, so a normal result does not exclude the syndrome.
activation.hyperventilation: Per protocol and the child's ability to cooperate.

recording.duration: Long enough to include sleep and, if the child is old enough, photic stimulation; repeat studies are common because the EEG evolves.
recording.montage: Standard pediatric montage with referential views for generalized and multifocal discharges. Use video to document each seizure type.

manifestations: Prolonged febrile or afebrile hemiclonic or generalized clonic seizures in the first year
Myoclonic, focal, atypical absence and tonic-clonic seizures appear later
Prolonged seizures and status epilepticus are common
Slowing of development after the first year, with gait and coordination problems
triggers: Photic or pattern stimulation in some
clinical.exam: Normal early; ataxia, hypotonia and crouch gait may develop later.
clinical.imaging: Usually normal at first; mild atrophy can appear later.
clinical.development: Normal in the first year, then slowing or plateau.

course.onset: First year of life, often around 6 months, with a febrile seizure.
course.progression: Several seizure types emerge in the next few years and the EEG background slows.
course.outcome: Usually drug-resistant seizures, intellectual disability and increased risk of early death, including sudden unexpected death.

differential: Simple febrile seizures - brief, with normal development and EEG
GEFS+ - febrile seizures plus, usually milder and with a better outcome
Lennox-Gastaut syndrome - later onset, with slow spike-wave and tonic seizures in sleep
Benign myoclonic epilepsy in infancy - normal development and a milder course
pearls: A first EEG in the first year is often normal, so repeat studies are common.
Fever, hot baths and illness can provoke seizures; record the temperature and any illness.
Photosensitivity can be present, so do photic stimulation carefully and be ready to stop.
Long seizures are common; document onset time, behavior and any need for the nurse or physician.
The usual cause is a gene (SCN1A) that is not seen on EEG; the technologist records only what is on the tracing.

syndromes.label: BMEI
syndromes.name: Myoclonic epilepsy in infancy (MEI, benign myoclonic epilepsy of infancy)
syndromes.ageText: Onset from about 4 months to 3 years, with a peak in the first 2 years
syndromes.seizure: Brief generalized myoclonic jerks of the head, trunk or arms, often in drowsiness or light sleep, in an otherwise normal infant
syndromes.pathophys: Presumed genetic in a developmentally normal child; the cause is not usually known. A reflex form triggered by sudden noise or touch exists.
syndromes.eeg: The background is normal for age. Brief generalized spike-wave or polyspike-wave bursts, usually 3 to 4 Hz and lasting a second or two, appear most often in drowsiness and light sleep and are often time-locked to a jerk. Discharges are usually rare or absent when the infant is fully awake.
syndromes.eegShort: Brief generalized spike-wave bursts in drowsiness and light sleep, with a normal background.
syndromes.technologist: Record drowsiness and light sleep, and use video and EMG to match any jerk to a burst. Time-mark every event and describe duration. Do not interpret the finding.

activation.sleep: Drowsiness and light sleep are the best states in which to capture bursts, so allow the infant to doze if possible.
activation.awake: Discharges may be sparse when the infant is fully awake.
activation.photic: Usually limited value; photic stimulation is done per the lab protocol.
activation.sleepDeprivation: Usually not needed in infants; a nap recording is the practical approach.

recording.duration: Long enough for a nap with drowsiness and light sleep, and a number of jerks if they occur.
recording.montage: Infant montage with a referential view for the generalized bursts. Add EMG leads and video, because jerks are brief and can be missed.

manifestations: Brief, bilateral myoclonic jerks of the head, arms or trunk
May cause a head nod or arm flexion, often when drowsy
Little or no loss of awareness
A reflex form triggered by sudden noise or touch can occur
triggers: Sudden noise or touch in the reflex form
clinical.development: Normal at onset; some children later show mild learning or behavioral difficulty.

course.onset: Infancy to early childhood.
course.progression: Seizures typically fade within a few years of onset; a minority later develop another generalized epilepsy.
course.outcome: Generally favorable seizure outcome, with follow-up of development advised.

differential: Dravet syndrome - febrile and prolonged seizures, several seizure types and developmental slowing
West syndrome - epileptic spasms with hypsarrhythmia and regression
Benign myoclonus of infancy - jerks with a normal EEG
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy - onset in adolescence
pearls: A normal infant with myoclonic jerks and brief generalized spike-wave bursts is the typical picture.
The tracing may be normal awake; drowsiness and light sleep are where bursts are found.
A jerk with no EEG correlate is possible, so use video and EMG and mark every event.
Describe the tracing and the events; identifying the syndrome is the physician's decision.
A background that is slow or abnormal for age should be noted, because it argues against this syndrome.
syndromes.sceneNote: Drowsy 1.5-year-old with two brief generalized spike-wave bursts of about 1.2 s each at 3.4 to 3.8 Hz.

syndromes.label: Doose (MAE)
syndromes.name: Epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures (Doose syndrome)
syndromes.classification: Generalized epilepsy syndrome (may have a DEE course)
syndromes.seizure: Myoclonic-atonic seizures (a jerk followed by a drop), with other generalized seizure types such as atypical absences and generalized tonic-clonic seizures
syndromes.pathophys: A genetically heterogeneous generalized epilepsy with a family history of generalized epilepsy in many; in some children specific genes are found.
syndromes.eeg: Usually begins with a normal background, which may then show bursts of rhythmic 4 to 7 Hz theta over the parietal region. Generalized spike-wave and polyspike-wave discharges (about 2 to 3 Hz) accompany myoclonic-atonic events. Slowing and non-convulsive status may appear.
syndromes.eegShort: Parietal rhythmic theta bursts then generalized spike-wave around 2.5 Hz.
syndromes.technologist: Record clinical jerks and falls with time marks, add a muscle (EMG) channel if possible, and describe background, theta bursts and discharge frequency.

activation.hyperventilation: Usually not feasible in this age group.
activation.sleep: May activate discharges; record wake and sleep.
activation.awake: Events and discharges can occur awake without provocation.

recording.duration: Include wake and sleep and try to capture events.
recording.montage: Referential and bipolar views; add EMG to document myoclonus and atonia.

manifestations: Sudden jerks with a head or body drop
Frequent falls and injuries
Atypical absences and generalized tonic-clonic seizures
Episodes of non-convulsive status
clinical.development: Often normal at onset; may decline.

course.onset: Early childhood, in a child who was developing normally.
course.progression: Variable; seizures may stop or persist.
course.outcome: Variable: some remit with normal or near-normal development, others have persisting seizures and cognitive impairment.

differential: Lennox-Gastaut syndrome - tonic seizures, slow spike-wave and fast bursts in sleep, usually delayed
Benign myoclonic epilepsy in infancy - myoclonic only, earlier, usually favourable
Dravet syndrome - earlier, febrile or hemiclonic seizures, developmental delay
Atypical absence in other DEEs
pearls: Rhythmic 4 to 7 Hz parietal theta may be a key background finding.
The classic seizure is a myoclonic jerk followed by an atonic drop.
Tonic seizures and fast bursts in sleep point instead toward Lennox-Gastaut.
The course may be favourable or evolve to a Lennox-Gastaut-like picture.
syndromes.sceneNote: The tracing shows bursts of rhythmic 5.5 Hz parietal theta, followed by generalized spike-wave at about 2.4 to 2.8 Hz, in an awake 3-year-old.

syndromes.name: Lennox-Gastaut syndrome
syndromes.seizure: Several types: tonic (often in sleep), atonic drop attacks, atypical absences; cognitive impairment
syndromes.pathophys: A diffuse developmental and epileptic encephalopathy from many causes (including prior West syndrome) in which networks are persistently disturbed.
syndromes.eeg: A slow background with bursts of slow (below 2.5 Hz, often 1.5 to 2.5 Hz) generalized spike-and-wave in wakefulness, and bursts of generalized paroxysmal fast activity (10 to 20 Hz) in non-REM sleep, which may accompany a brief tonic seizure or be subclinical.
syndromes.technologist: Record both waking and sleep. Mark clinical events with time and describe any fast bursts.
syndromes.label: Lennox-Gastaut
syndromes.eegShort: Slow spike-wave when awake and generalized fast bursts in sleep, on a slow background.

activation.sleep: The most informative state: generalized paroxysmal fast activity emerges in non-REM sleep and may accompany a brief tonic seizure or be subclinical.
activation.awake: Slow spike-and-wave is present while awake and may run in long bursts with drowsiness or inattention.
activation.hyperventilation: Usually not feasible and not particularly useful.

recording.duration: Long enough to include wake and sleep; clinical events should be captured if possible.
recording.montage: Use bipolar and referential views; adding a muscle (EMG) channel can help show a tonic seizure.

manifestations: Several seizure types: tonic (often in sleep), atonic drop attacks, atypical absences
Myoclonic, tonic-clonic and non-convulsive status may also occur
Intellectual disability or regression that tends to be persistent
Seizures are frequent and difficult to control
clinical.exam: Often abnormal, with cognitive and sometimes motor findings.
clinical.imaging: Often shows a cause such as structural malformation, injury or past encephalopathy.
clinical.development: Delay or regression is typical.

course.onset: Early to mid childhood; in some children it follows West syndrome.
course.progression: Chronic, with persisting seizures and cognitive impairment.
course.outcome: Generally poor long-term outcome.

differential: Doose syndrome - myoclonic-atonic seizures, onset often with normal development, tonic seizures rare early
Atypical absence in other DEEs - an isolated seizure type, not the full syndrome
CAE - faster 3 Hz spike-wave on a normal background, preserved cognition
DEE-SWAS (ESES) - spike-wave mostly in sleep, with regression
pearls: Slow spike-and-wave in wake plus generalized paroxysmal fast activity in sleep is the classic pair.
Paroxysmal fast activity may be subtle; a muscle channel and the observer's notes help confirm a tonic seizure.
Describe the awake and sleep background as slowed and note any asymmetry.
Hyperventilation can be a poor choice in this population; note when it was not performed and why.
syndromes.sceneNote: Two tracings are attached: slow generalized spike-and-wave in wake on a slow background, and a burst of generalized paroxysmal fast activity in non-REM sleep.

syndromes.label: Atypical absence
syndromes.name: Atypical absence seizures (typically within Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and other DEEs)
syndromes.classification: Seizure type seen in DEEs (for example Lennox-Gastaut)
syndromes.ageText: Early childhood onset, usually 1 to 8 years
syndromes.seizure: Staring with less abrupt onset and offset than a typical absence, often with partial loss of awareness and loss of tone
syndromes.pathophys: A seizure type of diffuse developmental and epileptic encephalopathies, reflecting widely disturbed networks rather than a single focus.
syndromes.eeg: Irregular, slow generalized spike-and-wave (about 2 to 2.5 Hz or less) on a slowed or disorganized background, often asymmetric and with a gradual start and end. Discharges are usually more prominent in drowsiness and non-REM sleep.
syndromes.eegShort: Slow irregular generalized spike-and-wave on a slow background.
syndromes.technologist: Describe the background, the discharge frequency and how it starts and stops. Record both waking and sleep, test responsiveness, and mark time and clinical features.

activation.sleep: Discharges are often more abundant in drowsiness and non-REM sleep; a sleep record is essential.
activation.awake: Slow spike-and-wave is present while awake, especially in drowsiness.

recording.duration: Include wake, drowsiness and sleep.
recording.montage: Referential and bipolar views to describe distribution and asymmetry.

manifestations: Slower onset and offset than typical absence
Partial change in responsiveness with tone loss, head drop or automatisms
Other seizure types, often tonic or atonic
Cognitive impairment and developmental delay
clinical.imaging: Often shows a structural or other cause.
clinical.development: Often delayed or regressed.

course.onset: Early childhood.
course.progression: Persisting seizures, usually within a long-lasting epilepsy syndrome.
course.outcome: Generally depends on the underlying syndrome and tends to be poor.

differential: Typical absence (CAE) - abrupt, regular 3 Hz, normal background
Jeavons syndrome - eyelid myoclonia with eye closure triggering
Focal impaired-awareness seizures - focal onset
Lennox-Gastaut syndrome - atypical absence is one of several seizure types
pearls: Slow generalized spike-and-wave (below 3 Hz) with gradual onset distinguishes it from typical absence.
The background is slowed, unlike CAE.
Sleep recording is important.
syndromes.sceneNote: The tracing shows irregular, slow generalized spike-and-wave at about 2 to 2.4 Hz on a slowed awake background in a 7-year-old.

syndromes.name: Self-limited epilepsy with autonomic seizures (SeLEAS, Panayiotopoulos syndrome)
syndromes.seizure: Autonomic seizures with vomiting, pallor and eye deviation, often in sleep and often prolonged
syndromes.pathophys: Hyperexcitable immature posterior cortex and autonomic networks; usually remits with age.
syndromes.eeg: Occipital spikes, often high amplitude with a following slow wave, that appear with eye closure and darkness and may disappear when the eyes are open (fixation-off sensitivity). Spikes can also appear in other regions.
syndromes.technologist: Record eyes closed and open in alternating periods, and note the effect of eye opening on the spikes.
syndromes.label: Occipital (Panayiotopoulos)
syndromes.eegShort: Occipital spikes that change with eye opening and closure.

activation.awake: Eye closure and darkness bring out occipital spikes; they may vanish with eyes open (fixation-off sensitivity), so alternate eyes-open and eyes-closed periods.
activation.sleep: Strongly activating; spikes often multiply and may appear in other regions.
activation.photic: Usually not specific; the key manoeuvre is eye closure, not flicker.

recording.duration: Include several eyes-open and eyes-closed periods and drowsiness or sleep.
recording.montage: Use bipolar and referential views including the posterior chain; document spikes in other regions too.

manifestations: Autonomic seizures: vomiting, pallor, flushing or incontinence
Eyes and head deviate to one side
Reduced responsiveness; events may last many minutes
Often begins in sleep; can progress to convulsive features
triggers: Illness or fever may precede some events
clinical.development: Usually normal.

course.onset: Preschool age, often around 3 to 6 years.
course.progression: Seizures are usually infrequent, and a few children have only one.
course.outcome: Self-limited, with remission within a few years of onset.

differential: Rolandic epilepsy - centrotemporal rather than occipital spikes, brief seizures with facial signs
Childhood occipital visual epilepsy (Gastaut type) - later onset, brief visual hallucinations, headache
Structural occipital epilepsy - fixed focus, abnormal imaging
Migraine or gastro-intestinal illness can mimic the vomiting events
pearls: Occipital spikes that appear on eye closure and disappear on eye opening show fixation-off sensitivity.
Spikes are not limited to the occipital region; multifocal spikes are common.
Document what the eyes were doing: open, closed, or fixating.
Sleep brings out discharges, so a drowsy or sleep recording is worth obtaining.
syndromes.sceneNote: The tracing shows occipital spikes whose appearance changes with eye opening and closure.

syndromes.name: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy with spike-and-wave activation in sleep (DEE-SWAS; ESES/CSWS) and Landau-Kleffner syndrome
syndromes.seizure: Variable seizures; regression of language, behaviour or cognition. In Landau-Kleffner syndrome, an acquired loss of language comprehension.
syndromes.pathophys: Persistent epileptiform activity in non-REM sleep disturbs the cortical networks that support learning and language.
syndromes.eeg: Near-continuous generalized or diffuse spike-and-wave (about 1.5 to 2.5 Hz) during non-REM sleep, occupying most of non-REM sleep. It is much less abundant while awake. The amount of spike-wave in sleep is measured by the reader.
syndromes.technologist: A sleep recording is essential. Describe how much of the sleep record shows discharges; do not stop early.
syndromes.label: ESES / LKS
syndromes.eegShort: Near-continuous spike-wave in non-REM sleep.

activation.sleep: Essential: the pattern is defined in non-REM sleep, and it is much less prominent in wakefulness and REM sleep.
activation.awake: The waking record may show only focal or generalized spikes, or look unremarkable.

recording.duration: Obtain a sleep record covering wake, drowsiness and a good stretch of non-REM sleep; do not stop early.
recording.montage: Bipolar and referential views are both useful; in LKS, note any temporal predominance.

manifestations: Regression or plateau in cognition, behaviour or attention
Seizures may be few, infrequent or absent, and may be focal, generalized or atypical absences
Landau-Kleffner syndrome: acquired loss of understanding of spoken language (auditory verbal agnosia) with later expressive loss
Behaviour change, including hyperactivity and attention problems
clinical.exam: May be normal apart from cognitive, language or behavioural deficits.
clinical.imaging: Often normal, but a structural cause is sometimes found.
clinical.development: Usually normal before onset, followed by regression.

course.onset: School-age children, with LKS often presenting with language loss in early school years.
course.progression: The sleep EEG picture usually fades with age, but the cognitive effects may lag behind.
course.outcome: Variable; a longer period of near-continuous discharge is linked with poorer recovery of language and cognition.

differential: Rolandic epilepsy - centrotemporal spikes in sleep but not near-continuous, normal cognition
Lennox-Gastaut - slow spike-wave in wake and fast bursts in sleep, multiple seizure types
Autism spectrum or developmental language disorder - no acquired loss of previously normal skills
Normal sleep activity - spike-wave persisting through non-REM sleep is not normal
pearls: The defining pattern appears during non-REM sleep, so a sleep study is essential.
The reader measures the proportion of non-REM sleep occupied by spike-wave; describe how much of the sleep record it fills.
Comparison with the waking record is valuable.
LKS is a language-regression presentation within this spectrum, and its discharges often favour the temporal regions.
The child may have few or no clinical seizures despite a very abnormal sleep EEG.
syndromes.sceneNote: The tracing shows near-continuous generalized spike-and-wave at about 2 Hz during non-REM sleep.

syndromes.name: Childhood absence epilepsy
syndromes.seizure: Brief staring spells with abrupt onset and offset, with or without eyelid flutter or automatisms, many times a day
syndromes.pathophys: Abnormal oscillation of the thalamocortical loop, involving T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons and GABA-B-mediated inhibition of relay neurons by the reticular nucleus, producing regular 3 Hz generalized spike-and-wave.
syndromes.eeg: A normal background with bursts of generalized, bilaterally synchronous 3 Hz (2.5 to 4 Hz) spike-and-wave, frontal predominant, lasting 4 to 20 seconds (the frontal maximum is clearest in referential montages; in bipolar chains the largest deflections are often centroparietal). The rate may slow slightly toward the end. Occipital intermittent rhythmic delta can occur. Hyperventilation is the best activation.
syndromes.technologist: Test responsiveness during bursts and note the time and what was said. Hyperventilation is done for the full protocol time if the patient can cooperate, and is stopped for a prolonged seizure or distress.
syndromes.label: Childhood absence
syndromes.eegShort: Generalized 3 Hz spike-and-wave on a normal background.

activation.hyperventilation: The most effective activation; often provokes typical absences in untreated children, so record it carefully.
activation.photic: Usually of limited value in this syndrome.
activation.sleep: Spike-wave may fragment or become faster and polyspike-like in non-REM sleep; absence seizures themselves do not occur in sleep.
activation.sleepDeprivation: May increase the chance of capturing discharges.
activation.awake: Include both eyes-open and eyes-closed periods.

recording.duration: A routine awake recording with full hyperventilation, plus drowsiness or sleep if the study allows.
recording.montage: Show both referential and bipolar views: the generalized, frontally predominant field is clearest referentially.

manifestations: Brief staring spells with abrupt onset and offset and impaired awareness
Eyelid flutter or simple automatisms may occur
Many events a day, no post-event confusion
No prominent eyelid myoclonia and no limb myoclonic jerks (this separates it from Jeavons and JME)
clinical.development: Usually normal; mild learning or attention difficulties are described.

course.onset: Early school age; absences begin in an otherwise normal child.
course.progression: Absences often fade in adolescence, though some patients go on to other generalized seizure types.
course.outcome: Often favourable, with remission in many; outcome is less certain if other seizure types appear.

differential: Juvenile absence epilepsy - later onset, absences less frequent, generalized tonic-clonic seizures more likely, spike-wave often a little faster
Epilepsy with eyelid myoclonia (Jeavons) - eyelid myoclonia, eye-closure and photic sensitivity
Atypical absence in LGS or other DEEs - slower spike-wave, gradual onset and offset, slowed background, cognitive impairment
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy - myoclonic jerks, polyspike-wave, adolescent onset
Very early-onset absences (before about 4 years) call for a wider look, for example GLUT1 deficiency, rather than assuming CAE
pearls: Hyperventilation is the key activation procedure for CAE; document effort, duration and the time to the first burst.
The spike-wave is generalized, bilaterally synchronous and symmetric, on a normal background.
Test and describe responsiveness during every burst, and note the time.
A normal background and normal development separate CAE from symptomatic generalized epilepsies.
syndromes.sceneNote: The tracing shows a generalized, synchronous 3 Hz spike-and-wave burst on an otherwise normal awake background.

syndromes.label: Eyelid myoclonia (Jeavons)
syndromes.name: Epilepsy with eyelid myoclonia (Jeavons syndrome)
syndromes.seizure: Brief eyelid myoclonia, often with upward eye deviation, with or without a short absence, usually triggered by eye closure and often by light
syndromes.pathophys: A genetic generalized epilepsy with marked cortical sensitivity to eye closure and to light, involving thalamocortical networks.
syndromes.eeg: Generalized spike-wave or polyspike-wave bursts at about 3 to 6 Hz that appear immediately after eye closure and are often accompanied by eyelid myoclonia. Photoparoxysmal responses are common. The background is usually normal.
syndromes.eegShort: Generalized spike-wave bursts that follow eye closure, often photosensitive.
syndromes.technologist: Repeat eye closure several times, each with a time mark, and see whether discharges follow within seconds. Keep photic stimulation to protocol, and describe eyelid movements clinically and in the notes.

activation.hyperventilation: May help but is not the main trigger.
activation.photic: Often provokes generalized discharges, but test carefully following protocol.
activation.sleep: Discharges often become less prominent in sleep.
activation.awake: Eye closure is the key manoeuvre; bursts often follow within a few seconds.

recording.duration: Include repeated eye-opening and eye-closure periods.
recording.montage: Referential and bipolar views; include a frontal or eyelid channel if possible to document eyelid movement.

manifestations: Rapid rhythmic eyelid jerks with upward eye deviation
Often brief absence with impaired awareness
Seizures often follow eye closure or bright light and may occur many times a day
Patients may deliberately close their eyes to trigger events
clinical.development: Usually normal; some have learning difficulties.

course.onset: Early to mid childhood.
course.progression: Eyelid myoclonia often persists, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures can appear.
course.outcome: Often lifelong and may be hard to control; photosensitivity can improve with age.

differential: Childhood absence epilepsy - no eyelid myoclonia, generalized 3 Hz spike-wave without eye closure triggering
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy - limb jerks on waking
Eye-closure-sensitive generalized epilepsy without eyelid myoclonia
Occipital epilepsy - occipital spikes rather than generalized bursts
pearls: Discharges follow eye closure, usually within a few seconds, and the record may show repeated bursts after each closure.
Photosensitivity is common but not universal.
Eyelid myoclonia is a clinical observation; document it in the technologist notes.
Compare eyes-open and eyes-closed periods carefully.
syndromes.sceneNote: The tracing shows two episodes of generalized 4 to 5 Hz spike-wave bursts beginning right after eye closure, with eyes open at 5.0 seconds in between.

syndromes.label: Eye closure sensitivity
syndromes.name: Eye-closure sensitivity (reflex trait in genetic generalized epilepsy)
syndromes.classification: Reflex trait, not a separate ILAE syndrome
syndromes.seizure: Brief absences or myoclonic events triggered by eye closure, sometimes with eyelid myoclonia
syndromes.pathophys: A reflex trait of generalized epilepsies in which eye closure triggers generalized discharges, probably through cortical hyperexcitability; it overlaps strongly with epilepsy with eyelid myoclonia.
syndromes.eeg: Generalized spike-wave bursts (about 3 to 4.5 Hz, sometimes polyspike) that appear within seconds of eye closure, often in repeated episodes with eyes open in between. The background is usually normal.
syndromes.eegShort: Generalized spike-wave bursts right after eye closure.
syndromes.technologist: Repeat eye closure several times, each with a time mark. Note whether discharges follow, how soon, and whether they stop with eyes open.

activation.awake: Eye closure is the key activation and should be repeated several times; compare with the eyes-open record.
activation.photic: Eyes-closed photic stimulation may add to the response; follow protocol.
activation.sleep: Discharges often decrease in sleep.

recording.duration: Include several eye-opening and eye-closure periods.
recording.montage: Referential and bipolar views.

manifestations: Absences or brief myoclonic events right after eye closure
Eyelid myoclonia in some
Photosensitivity in some
Patients may self-induce events
clinical.development: Usually normal.

course.onset: Childhood to early adolescence.
course.progression: Variable.
course.outcome: Variable; sensitivity may persist.

differential: Jeavons syndrome - eyelid myoclonia is prominent
CAE or JAE - absences are not tied to eye closure
Occipital epilepsy - occipital spikes with fixation-off sensitivity
Other photosensitive epilepsies - triggered by light itself
pearls: Bursts appear soon after eye closure rather than during hyperventilation.
Repeated closures confirm the relationship.
Mark each closure and each burst with time.
Document whether the eyes were open or closed when the discharge stopped.
syndromes.sceneNote: The tracing shows two episodes of generalized 3.6 to 4.2 Hz spike-wave bursts right after eye closure in an awake 9-year-old.

syndromes.name: Self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (rolandic epilepsy)
syndromes.seizure: Nocturnal or on waking: hemifacial twitching, speech arrest, drooling, sometimes spreading to the arm or generalizing
syndromes.pathophys: Hyperexcitable perisylvian sensorimotor cortex in an immature brain; resolves in adolescence.
syndromes.eeg: Normal background. High-amplitude biphasic centrotemporal spikes (C3, C4, T3, T4) with a horizontal dipole: negative centrally and positive frontally. Sleep strongly activates them, and they may shift sides.
syndromes.technologist: Record sleep. Use referential and transverse montages to show the dipole; mention side shifts.
syndromes.label: Rolandic
syndromes.eegShort: Centrotemporal spikes with a horizontal dipole, activated by sleep.

activation.sleep: The strongest activator: spikes become more frequent in drowsiness and non-REM sleep and may spread or become bilateral.
activation.sleepDeprivation: May help if a routine awake record is normal.
activation.awake: Spikes may be sparse or absent when awake, so a normal waking record does not exclude the syndrome.

recording.duration: Include drowsiness and sleep; a waking-only record can miss the discharges.
recording.montage: Use referential and bipolar/transverse views to show the dipole: negative centrotemporally, positive frontally. Report any shift between hemispheres.

manifestations: Unilateral facial twitching or sensory change around the mouth
Speech arrest, gurgling noises and drooling
Often at night or on waking; may spread to the arm or become bilateral tonic-clonic
Awareness is often preserved in waking events
clinical.development: Usually normal; mild language, attention or learning difficulties can occur.

course.onset: School age, usually between about 3 and 14 years.
course.progression: Seizures are infrequent in many children and fade with age.
course.outcome: Self-limited, with remission by mid-adolescence; a minority show atypical features or a spike-wave-in-sleep picture.

differential: Panayiotopoulos syndrome - occipital or multifocal spikes, autonomic seizures with vomiting
DEE-SWAS (ESES/CSWS) - spike-wave takes up most of non-REM sleep, with regression
Structural focal epilepsy - fixed focus, abnormal exam or imaging
Centrotemporal spikes are also seen in some children who never have seizures, so the EEG alone is not diagnostic
pearls: Centrotemporal spikes are strongly activated by sleep; record drowsiness and sleep.
The spike is high amplitude, diphasic, with an aftergoing slow wave and a horizontal dipole.
The background is normal and the discharges can shift sides or be bilateral independent.
Mark any spike-wave that becomes near-continuous in sleep and describe how much of the sleep record it occupies.
syndromes.sceneNote: The tracing shows high-amplitude centrotemporal spikes with a horizontal dipole on a normal background.

syndromes.name: Frontal lobe epilepsy
syndromes.seizure: Brief frequent seizures, often from sleep, with hypermotor or tonic posturing and little confusion afterward
syndromes.pathophys: Cortical malformation, tumour or injury, or a genetic cause (for example autosomal dominant sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy, formerly nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy) in a large, deep and highly connected lobe.
syndromes.eeg: Interictal spikes may be absent or are frontal, with rapid bilateral spread. Frontal spikes show a phase reversal at the frontal electrode over the focus (F3 or F4) in the longitudinal chain, and at the same electrode in the transverse chain when it lies mid-chain. Ictal EEG is often obscured by muscle and movement artifact.
syndromes.technologist: Document the clinical event carefully with video. Artifact makes the ictal tracing hard to read, so mark the event time precisely.
syndromes.label: Frontal lobe
syndromes.eegShort: Frontal spikes, often scarce; rapid bilateral spread.

activation.sleep: Sleep often increases frontal discharges; record it when allowed.
activation.sleepDeprivation: May increase the chance of capturing spikes or an event.
activation.awake: A waking record is often normal or shows only subtle changes.

recording.duration: Seizures are brief and frequent, so a prolonged record or video-EEG that captures sleep may be needed.
recording.montage: Longitudinal and transverse bipolar chains, plus a referential montage. Add frontal and mesial coverage if the protocol allows.

manifestations: Brief seizures, often several a day or night, usually from sleep
Hypermotor movements, tonic posturing or vocalization
Preserved or rapidly recovered awareness with little postictal confusion
Seizures can be mistaken for non-epileptic events or parasomnias
clinical.imaging: Often normal, but a cortical malformation, tumour or injury may be seen.
clinical.development: Usually normal; depends on the cause.

course.onset: Any age.
course.progression: Depends on the cause; seizures often cluster in sleep.
course.outcome: Variable; medication-resistant cases may be evaluated for surgery.

differential: Temporal lobe epilepsy - aura, longer events, automatisms and postictal confusion
Non-epileptic or psychogenic events - no EEG change, but remember that frontal seizures can have a normal scalp EEG
Sleep parasomnias - not clustered in the same stereotyped way
Generalized epilepsy - symmetric generalized bursts rather than a frontal focus
pearls: Scalp EEG can be normal or obscured by muscle and movement, so video and exact timing matter.
Frontal spikes may spread rapidly and appear bilateral, which can look generalized.
Seizures are brief, stereotyped and often arise from sleep.
Phase reversal at F3 or F4 in the longitudinal chain locates a frontal spike.
Mark the event with the clock time and describe the motor behaviour (for example posturing, thrashing, vocalization) and the patient's responsiveness.

syndromes.label: IGE
syndromes.name: Genetic generalized epilepsies (formerly idiopathic generalized epilepsies), overview
syndromes.ageText: Childhood to young adulthood, depending on the syndrome
syndromes.seizure: Absence, myoclonic and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, in different combinations by syndrome
syndromes.pathophys: A group of epilepsies with a strong genetic contribution and no structural cause, in which thalamo-cortical networks produce brief generalized discharges.
syndromes.eeg: Normal background with generalized, symmetric, synchronous spike-and-wave or polyspike-and-wave bursts. The rate differs by syndrome: about 3 Hz in childhood absence epilepsy, faster and with polyspikes in JME, and quicker (often 4 to 5 Hz) in eyelid myoclonia with absences. Discharges are often more frequent in drowsiness, with sleep fragmenting them.
syndromes.eegShort: Generalized spike-wave and polyspike-wave on a normal background.
syndromes.technologist: Choose activation for the likely syndrome as the request and protocol direct: hyperventilation and photic stimulation per protocol, plus sleep. Describe the discharges (rate, distribution, duration) and test responsiveness during bursts.

activation.hyperventilation: The most effective activation for childhood absence epilepsy; less so for JME.
activation.photic: Especially relevant in eyelid myoclonia with absences and in photosensitive patients; less so in childhood absence.
activation.sleepDeprivation: Often helpful, especially in the syndromes with convulsions or jerks on waking such as JME.
activation.sleep: Discharges are often more frequent in drowsiness and on waking; the bursts fragment in deeper sleep.
activation.awake: A routine awake record is often normal between seizures.

recording.duration: Long enough for the planned activation and, when requested, sleep.
recording.montage: Referential and bipolar views to show the generalized distribution.

manifestations: Typical absence: brief staring with loss of awareness
Myoclonic jerks, usually on waking
Generalized tonic-clonic seizures
A normal neurological exam and development are typical
clinical.development: Usually normal.

course.onset: Childhood to young adulthood; the age is the best clue to the syndrome.
course.progression: Depends on the syndrome; some remit with age, others persist for life.
course.outcome: Most patients have a good outlook; the syndromes differ in how long treatment is needed.

differential: Symptomatic or developmental generalized epilepsy (e.g. Lennox-Gastaut) - abnormal background and slow generalized discharges
Focal epilepsy with bilateral spread - asymmetric onset or focal spikes
Progressive myoclonus epilepsies - slowed background and progressive decline
Non-epileptic events - no epileptiform change
pearls: IGE is an umbrella for childhood absence epilepsy, juvenile absence epilepsy, JME and GTCA, with eyelid myoclonia with absences sometimes grouped with them.
Match the activation to the likely syndrome: hyperventilation for absence, photic for photosensitive syndromes, sleep deprivation and awakening for JME.
Generalized, symmetric, synchronous discharges on a normal background separate IGE from focal and symptomatic epilepsies.
Count the rate of the burst: about 3 Hz fits childhood absence, faster rates and polyspikes suggest older-onset syndromes.

Current ILAE (2022) limits the IGE group to childhood absence, juvenile absence, juvenile myoclonic and generalized tonic-clonic seizures alone; eyelid myoclonia with absences is a related generalized epilepsy syndrome.
syndromes.sceneNote: Awake 12-year-old with a generalized 3.8 to 4.2 Hz spike-wave burst and a polyspike-wave complex.

syndromes.name: Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy
syndromes.seizure: Rising epigastric aura, fear or deja vu, then staring, lip-smacking and hand automatisms with impaired awareness and later confusion
syndromes.pathophys: Often hippocampal sclerosis, with neuronal loss and sprouting that make the circuit hyperexcitable.
syndromes.eeg: Interictal anterior temporal sharp waves with a maximum at F7/F8 or an anterior temporal electrode, more frequent in drowsiness and sleep, often with temporal slowing. Ictal onset is rhythmic theta (about 5 to 7 Hz) that grows in amplitude, slows and spreads to adjacent regions.
syndromes.technologist: Record sleep. Use the longitudinal chain to show the phase reversal at F7/F8 (Fp1-F7 and F7-T3), and a referential montage to show that F7 or F8 has the largest amplitude. During a seizure test responsiveness and describe behaviour.
syndromes.label: Mesial TLE
syndromes.eegShort: Anterior temporal sharp waves; ictal rhythmic theta.

activation.sleep: Drowsiness and light sleep often bring out or increase temporal sharp waves; record sleep if allowed.
activation.sleepDeprivation: Often helpful; may increase the chance of capturing spikes.
activation.awake: Waking spikes may be infrequent or absent, so a normal awake record does not exclude it.
activation.hyperventilation: Per protocol; it can enhance temporal slowing or spikes in some patients.

recording.duration: Long enough to include sleep; a longer or prolonged record increases the chance of capturing seizures.
recording.montage: Longitudinal and transverse bipolar chains to show phase reversal, plus a referential montage to show the field. Include the anterior temporal (T1/T2 or equivalent) electrodes if the protocol allows, because they can show spikes that standard electrodes miss.

manifestations: Aura: rising epigastric sensation, fear, deja vu or a smell
Behavioural arrest and staring with impaired awareness
Oral and hand automatisms, such as lip-smacking or fumbling
Contralateral dystonic posturing in some
Postictal confusion; may evolve to a bilateral tonic-clonic seizure
clinical.exam: Usually normal; memory complaints are common.
clinical.imaging: MRI may show hippocampal sclerosis (mesial temporal sclerosis) or another lesion.
clinical.development: Usually normal; a history of prolonged febrile seizures is common in the mesial form.

course.onset: Most often in later childhood or the teens, with a possible seizure-free interval earlier.
course.progression: Chronic; some patients stay refractory to medication and may be evaluated for surgery.
course.outcome: Variable; patients with hippocampal sclerosis often have refractory seizures.

differential: Frontal lobe epilepsy - brief hypermotor events, often from sleep, with little postictal confusion
Occipital or parietal epilepsy - visual or sensory features and posterior spikes
Non-epileptic events - no EEG change and variable semiology
Benign temporal variants (wicket spikes, small sharp spikes) - not slowed, no aftergoing slow wave and not clustered
pearls: Anterior temporal sharp waves are maximal at F7 or F8 and more frequent in drowsiness and sleep.
Phase reversal at F7/F8 in the longitudinal chain locates the spike; the referential montage confirms the field.
Ictal onset is often rhythmic theta that builds in amplitude and slows as it spreads.
During a seizure, test responsiveness and describe automatisms with times for the reader.
Hippocampal sclerosis is the classic pathology of the mesial form.

syndromes.label: Juvenile absence
syndromes.name: Juvenile absence epilepsy
syndromes.seizure: Typical absences, often less frequent than in childhood absence epilepsy, with generalized tonic-clonic seizures common and occasional myoclonic jerks
syndromes.pathophys: A genetically determined generalized epilepsy in which thalamocortical networks generate generalized spike-and-wave; the network mechanism overlaps with childhood absence epilepsy.
syndromes.eeg: Normal background with generalized, bilaterally synchronous spike-and-wave bursts, often slightly faster than 3 Hz (about 3.5 to 4.5 Hz) and sometimes with polyspikes. Bursts may last a few seconds to over 10 seconds.
syndromes.eegShort: Generalized spike-and-wave a little faster than 3 Hz on a normal background.
syndromes.technologist: Test responsiveness during bursts and note the time and what was said. Perform hyperventilation, and record both awake and drowsy or sleep states.

activation.hyperventilation: Often helpful for provoking bursts, though less reliably than in childhood absence.
activation.photic: Occasionally brings out discharges; use the full protocol.
activation.sleep: May increase discharges; generalized tonic-clonic seizures are more likely near awakening.
activation.sleepDeprivation: Often increases the chance of capturing discharges.
activation.awake: Bursts may appear without provocation.

recording.duration: Awake recording with hyperventilation and photic stimulation, plus drowsiness or sleep if possible.
recording.montage: Referential and bipolar views to show the generalized distribution.

manifestations: Impaired awareness with staring, usually without marked automatisms
Absences are less frequent than in childhood absence epilepsy and can last longer
Generalized tonic-clonic seizures are common, often near waking
Myoclonic jerks may occur
clinical.development: Usually normal.

course.onset: From about 8 years through the teens; peak around puberty.
course.progression: Absences tend to persist, and tonic-clonic seizures may continue into adulthood.
course.outcome: Often remains lifelong or needs long-term follow-up; less likely to remit than childhood absence epilepsy.

differential: Childhood absence epilepsy - younger onset, more frequent absences, regular 3 Hz
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy - myoclonic jerks on waking, polyspike-wave
Jeavons syndrome - eyelid myoclonia with eye closure sensitivity
Focal seizures with impaired awareness - different EEG and onset
pearls: The spike-and-wave is often a little faster than the 3 Hz of childhood absence.
Generalized tonic-clonic seizures are more common than in childhood absence epilepsy.
Hyperventilation and sleep-deprived studies are the usual activation tools.
syndromes.sceneNote: The tracing shows a generalized spike-and-wave burst at about 3.6 to 4 Hz lasting about 5.6 seconds in an awake 14-year-old.

syndromes.name: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
syndromes.seizure: Myoclonic jerks, especially soon after waking; generalized tonic-clonic seizures; absences in some
syndromes.pathophys: A genetic generalized epilepsy with a hyperexcitable frontal-thalamic network. Sleep deprivation, alcohol and flashing lights lower the threshold.
syndromes.eeg: Normal background with brief generalized polyspike-and-slow-wave complexes (a burst of 4 to 6 Hz polyspike-wave may repeat for 1 to 3 seconds), often frontal predominant, sometimes with a photoparoxysmal response. Bursts are often activated by sleep deprivation and by awakening.
syndromes.technologist: Record on waking or after sleep deprivation if requested. Mark jerks with the time. Photic stimulation per protocol, stopping at the first sign of a photoparoxysmal discharge.
syndromes.label: JME
syndromes.eegShort: Generalized 4 to 6 Hz polyspike-wave bursts, often frontal predominant.

activation.sleepDeprivation: Often very helpful. Recording soon after waking, when jerks and discharges are most likely, may increase the chance of capturing events.
activation.sleep: Include drowsiness and the awakening itself; discharges tend to cluster around sleep-wake transitions.
activation.photic: A photoparoxysmal response is seen in a sizeable minority. Run the protocol as written and stop at the first generalized discharge, because flashes can trigger a jerk or a convulsion.
activation.hyperventilation: Less productive than sleep deprivation, but still performed per protocol.

recording.duration: Long enough to include drowsiness, sleep and a documented awakening; a routine awake-only record may be normal.
recording.montage: Use both referential and bipolar views so the generalized, symmetric distribution and the frontal emphasis can be shown.

manifestations: Brief, bilateral, symmetric jerks of the shoulders and arms, most often shortly after waking; objects may be dropped
Generalized tonic-clonic seizures, often after waking or after sleep loss
Absence seizures in a minority
Consciousness is usually preserved during the jerks
clinical.development: Normal intelligence and development in most patients.

course.onset: Usually in the teenage years, with jerks often appearing before the first convulsion.
course.progression: A lifelong tendency; the tendency is lifelong.
course.outcome: Seizures are controlled in most patients with treatment, but a long-term course is typical.

differential: Childhood and juvenile absence epilepsy - absence is the main seizure type and there are no myoclonic jerks
Epilepsy with generalized tonic-clonic seizures alone - no jerks or absences
Progressive myoclonus epilepsies - abnormal exam, slowed background and a progressive course
Frontal lobe seizures - focal onset and asymmetric features rather than symmetric generalized bursts
pearls: The EEG finding to look for is generalized polyspike-and-wave, usually faster than the 3 Hz spike-and-wave of childhood absence epilepsy.
Jerks cluster after waking, so recording after sleep or at awakening is the key activation.
Mark the exact time of any jerk so the reader can match it to the polyspike burst.
Photic stimulation can provoke discharges and convulsions; stop at the first discharge.
The background is normal between bursts, which separates JME from symptomatic generalized epilepsy.

syndromes.label: GTCA
syndromes.name: Epilepsy with generalized tonic-clonic seizures alone (GTCA)
syndromes.ageText: Peak in adolescence; onset from about 5 to 40 years
syndromes.seizure: Generalized tonic-clonic seizures are the only seizure type, often shortly after waking or from sleep
syndromes.pathophys: A genetic generalized epilepsy in which cortico-thalamic networks are hyperexcitable. Sleep loss, alcohol and fatigue lower the threshold.
syndromes.eeg: Normal background with brief generalized spike-and-wave or polyspike-and-wave bursts, typically 3 to 6 Hz, symmetric and synchronous. Discharges are often more frequent in drowsiness and after waking. During a convulsion, the tonic phase brings generalized fast activity, followed by rhythmic bursts and then postictal slowing.
syndromes.eegShort: Generalized 3 to 6 Hz spike-wave and polyspike-wave on a normal background.
syndromes.technologist: Record drowsiness, sleep and an awakening if the protocol allows. Perform activation per protocol and mark any clinical event with its time. If a convulsion occurs, keep the patient safe, describe the onset and the behaviour, and keep recording through the postictal period.

activation.sleepDeprivation: Often helpful; recording after sleep loss and around awakening may increase the chance of capturing discharges.
activation.sleep: Include drowsiness and the awakening, since discharges and seizures cluster there.
activation.hyperventilation: Per protocol; it may bring out generalized discharges.
activation.photic: Per protocol; a photoparoxysmal response is less typical than in JME but is possible.
activation.awake: A waking record may be normal or show only occasional bursts.

recording.duration: Long enough to include sleep and awakening; a short awake record can be normal.
recording.montage: Use referential and bipolar views to show the generalized, symmetric distribution.

manifestations: Generalized tonic-clonic seizure with loss of awareness, stiffening, then rhythmic jerking
Seizures often occur soon after waking or during sleep
By definition no absence seizures or myoclonic jerks (a careful history is needed to be sure)
clinical.development: Normal.

course.onset: Mostly in the second decade, with a wide range.
course.progression: Variable; some patients stay free of seizures, in others the tendency persists.
course.outcome: Seizures are controlled in many patients; some patients later reveal myoclonic or absence seizures, which changes the syndrome label.

differential: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy - the history includes myoclonic jerks, and polyspike-wave is usually present
Childhood or juvenile absence epilepsy - absence seizures are a defining feature
Focal epilepsy with secondary generalization - focal onset or focal spikes, and asymmetry
Convulsive syncope or non-epileptic events - no epileptiform change on EEG
pearls: GTCA means convulsions only: no absences and no myoclonic jerks.
Seizures cluster around awakening, so recording drowsiness and the awakening adds value.
The interictal EEG may be normal; a normal record does not exclude the syndrome.
During a convulsion, muscle artifact hides the cortical rhythm, so the clinical description and timing carry the information.
The normal background and normal exam and imaging separate it from symptomatic generalized epilepsy.
syndromes.sceneNote: Awake 17-year-old with a generalized 4 to 4.6 Hz spike-wave burst and a polyspike-wave complex on a normal background.

patterns.name: Lateralized periodic discharges (LPDs, formerly PLEDs) in a focal destructive illness
patterns.context: For example acute herpes simplex encephalitis involving one temporal lobe
patterns.eeg: Periodic sharp or sharp-and-slow complexes about every 1 to 2 seconds, lateralized to the affected temporal region, over focal delta and slowing.
patterns.pathophys: Acute necrosis of cortex and deafferentation produce stereotyped repeating discharges.
patterns.technologist: Describe the interval between complexes and the side, record state and medications, and tell the reader promptly if the pattern changes.

patterns.name: Generalized periodic discharges (GPDs) in a rapidly progressive dementia
patterns.eeg: Stereotyped bi- or triphasic sharp complexes repeating about once per second, generalized and usually fairly symmetric (they can be asymmetric early), on a slowed background. They may disappear in very advanced disease.
patterns.pathophys: Widespread cortical neuronal loss and spongiform change, with synchronous bursts of activity.
patterns.technologist: Record stimulus responses (the complexes may be reduced by sedation). Describe the rate and distribution. Follow the facility prion policy: use disposable electrodes and supplies and do not reuse cup or needle electrodes.

patterns.name: Periodic complexes in subacute sclerosing panencephalitis
patterns.context: A late complication of measles in a child or adolescent, with myoclonic jerks
patterns.eeg: Stereotyped high-amplitude generalized complexes recurring every 4 to 10 seconds, often time-locked to a myoclonic jerk, on a slowed background.
patterns.pathophys: Persistent viral infection of the brain that damages cortex and white matter.
patterns.technologist: Use a long page (or time base) so the long interval is visible, and mark each jerk with the time.

patterns.name: Alpha coma
patterns.context: A comatose patient after cardiac arrest or with a brainstem lesion
patterns.eeg: Generalized alpha-range activity (8 to 12 Hz) that is frontally predominant and does not react to stimulation. The pattern is unlike a normal posterior alpha rhythm, which blocks with eye opening.
patterns.pathophys: A pathological rhythm produced by injured cortex and its brainstem or thalamic connections, which no longer respond to input.
patterns.technologist: Test and record reactivity with every protocol stimulus. Describe the distribution and frequency, and the medications and temperature if known.

patterns.name: Drug-induced beta activity
patterns.context: A patient taking a benzodiazepine or barbiturate
patterns.eeg: Excess beta (about 13 to 30 Hz), generalized and frontally predominant, often in an otherwise normal record. The posterior rhythm may be present or reduced.
patterns.pathophys: Enhanced GABA-A receptor activity changes the thalamocortical rhythms.
patterns.technologist: Record the medications and doses with their times. Describe the activity without naming the cause.

mistakes: The scalp EEG records action potentials.
It records summed postsynaptic potentials from synchronously active pyramidal neurons.
A small cortical focus will always show on the scalp.
A small area, or a focus deep in a sulcus or on the medial surface, can be invisible; several square centimetres of synchronous cortex are needed.
Delta waves always mean damage.
Delta is normal in deep sleep. Focal polymorphic delta while awake points to a focal lesion (often white matter) that has deafferented the cortex; the reader judges the cause.
A normal interictal EEG rules out epilepsy.
A single routine EEG shows epileptiform discharges in only about half of patients with epilepsy or fewer, and less often in frontal lobe epilepsy. Repeat studies and sleep raise the yield.
Absence seizures come from a single cortical focus.
They arise in an abnormal thalamocortical loop and produce generalized, symmetric discharges.
Hypsarrhythmia means the cause is known.
It is a pattern, not a diagnosis. Many causes produce it.
Rolandic spikes are always on one side.
They can shift sides and can be bilateral; sleep activates them.
Temporal lobe seizures start with generalized convulsions.
They typically start with an aura and automatisms; a generalized convulsion is a later spread.
The alpha rhythm in a comatose patient is a good sign.
Alpha that is frontally dominant and unreactive in coma (alpha coma) is a pathological pattern.
The technologist can name the syndrome from the EEG.
The reader interprets and diagnoses. The technologist describes with numbers, marks events and documents state and medications.

genetics.intro: Genes do not give an EEG pattern by themselves. Many genes cause the same pattern, and one gene can cause different patterns at different ages. Use this tab to link the age, the EEG and the associated signs to the conditions the reader may consider. A technologist records and describes; the reader and the clinician make the genetic diagnosis.
principles: One pattern, many genes: hypsarrhythmia and burst suppression have many genetic and non-genetic causes.
One gene, many patterns: the EEG changes with age, so the same gene can show burst suppression in a neonate and hypsarrhythmia later.
A normal EEG does not exclude a genetic disorder, especially for NF1, NF2 and the first study in SCN1A or CDKL5.
Skin, head size, behavior and movements are part of your report: describe them, and note how artifact from hand stereotypies, laughing or muscle appears.
patternTable: Nonspecific; other encephalopathies can look similar
Nonspecific: also seen with subdural fluid, infarct or scalp swelling; compare sides at equal sensitivity
Drugs also cause beta; check the history
The interictal EEG is often normal

items.label: Tuberous sclerosis
